results.summary: Every check must demonstrably go red when the condition it guards breaks; a green result that would also appear on a broken run is false assurance. Nine rules follow: no skip except transport failure, seeded ops need success assertions, negative assertions need positive controls, error checks must cite specific codes, reconciliation checks need independent operands, new gates get watched through their first full run, guards get tested against every mutation type, assertions target a specific subject not a broad pattern, and existing green tests get re-examined when a related bug is fixed.
results.origin_incident: Not stated in the fetched skill doc (it cites unnamed incident investigations where green signals masked unexecuted controls); not a datum-specific incident.
results.datum_evidence: FLOW.md §2 Act: "RED green-blindness" gate — the post-RED batch runs the suite and treats exit 0 as `green_blindness_violation`, i.e. it proves the new RED test can actually fail before trusting it. §5 Properties: "New verdict functions get a property before an example" and "'failed' implies evidence... absence is named, never 'clean' and never 'failed'" (fast-check/Hypothesis property tests on verdict functions) is the closest existing mechanism to a generalized "prove it can fail" contract, but it is scoped to verdict functions only, not to every gate/batch check.
results.proposal: Datum enforces this principle ad hoc, one closure at a time, rather than as a standing gate: §5's closed-gap list records at least four defects that are exactly "a check that cannot go red" — closeout's token collector wrote 0 for a run it never measured (6fdf8add), an empty verify reply read as a red suite instead of a named unavailable state (14948947/334e8739), Review's severity string comparison silently passed "High" vs "HIGH" (9f992b9a), and `gate_review`'s canMerge was LLM-judged and unreachable (b5528aa). The smallest concrete addition: extend the existing verdict-function property-testing convention (skills/src/shared/verdicts.property.test.ts, tests/test_gate_properties.py) into a static completeness test — analogous to `agent-types-ordering.test.ts` or `test_skill_bundles_have_consumers.py` — that walks every named-failure prefix `classifyLaneError` knows about and asserts a corresponding test exists that feeds the guarded function a broken/absent input and checks the named failure (not just "clean") is produced. This turns "new verdict functions get a property before an example" from a stated convention into an enforced batch step, closing the gap between the Properties section's stated policy and what CI actually checks.
results.where: Act phase / test-infrastructure layer: skills/src/shared/verdicts.property.test.ts, tests/test_gate_properties.py, plus a new completeness check alongside skills/src/shared/agent-types-ordering.test.ts or tests/test_skill_bundles_have_consumers.py.
results.rationale: The principle is already partially adopted (green-blindness gate, verdict property tests, "absence is named never clean" convention) and maps to a recorded pattern of FLOW.md §5 closures where an unfailable check masked a real defect, so it has real value; but it is not a single missing mechanism, it is an unenforced extension of an existing convention, so it is a small follow-up (one static test) rather than an urgent gap.

results.origin_incident: Documentation cites seven incidents where "every automated gate was green and the feature was broken in production," with failures living specifically in cross-layer seams.
results.datum_evidence: FLOW.md §5 Open/Closed gap list, closure "A conflicting lane merge lost its git-level reason": "...the browser gate for DOM/canvas lanes, which would have caught four defects every unit-level check missed, is #457." This is an explicitly named, still-open follow-up acknowledging exactly the seam this skill targets (unit/mocked verification passing while the real rendered artifact is broken) — datum's own dogfooding record (elonchesd browser game, epic-2, "the game plays in a browser" confirmed only by manual note, not a gate) independently surfaced the same class of defect the skill is built to prevent. Validate's gate (§2 Validate section) re-runs `config.test_command` deterministically but that is the same test command already run in-lane — never a real deployed/rendered/authenticated invocation.
results.proposal: Add a deterministic browser/runtime-verify batch step, gated the same way as every other Act/Validate check (agent proposes a DOM/canvas or user-facing classification on the lane; the batch step re-verifies by actually driving it): for lanes whose files/kind match a UI/rendered-output classification, Validate (or a dedicated post-REFACTOR check in Act) launches the real build artifact headless (e.g. Playwright against the actual dev/build target, not a mock), exercises the lane's acceptance-criteria path, and fails as a new named failure (e.g. `browser_verify_failed`) on non-zero exit or console error — never treated as advisory. This is the closure datum's own backlog already names as #457; scope it as a Validate-phase batch step over `shared/lane-steps.ts` / a new `browser-verify.ts`, not a new phase.
results.where: Validate phase (or Act's post-REFACTOR verify), skills/src/datum-validate.ts + skills/src/shared/lane-steps.ts, closing tracked issue #457
results.rationale: Datum already recognizes this exact defect class in FLOW.md §5 (unit-level checks missing four real defects, tracked as open issue #457) but has not implemented the gate — so the mechanism is genuinely partial, not fabricated from the skill alone. Cost is moderate (one new batch step + a lane classification, not a new phase or agent type), and it slots into the existing propose/verify pattern rather than requiring new architecture, so it is worth adopting once #457 is prioritized rather than immediately in this audit.

results.summary: A seven-step classification framework for when a suite flips from green to broadly red: find the causally-first failure, rule out rate limits, truncation, environment breakage, and out-of-diff blast radius before debugging, run twice to separate flake from regression, and instrument opaque skips. It classifies rather than fixes, converting long debugging into fast attribution.
results.origin_incident: Not stated explicitly; the framing implies a suite that went mass-red and was debugged as code defects when the cause was infrastructure.
results.datum_evidence: Most steps are covered by construction at the point of failure, not by after-the-fact triage: step 4 (environment) is `test_env_missing` (b1634731/97117202, lane worktrees with no node_modules/.venv made every verify exit 1); step 7 / "null is never failed" is `green_verify_unavailable` + `count_gate_no_output` (14948947/334e8739, an empty verify reply read as a red suite and blocked 17 dependents); step 1 (cascade) is the dep-blocked lane status, which triage never files; step 5 is the ownership/scope gates; `classifyLaneError` (00c3892) maps every named prefix deterministically, and 4da0c82c fixed a triage mis-attribution (#441). Step 3's counted-summary rule exists per-lane (`newTestCountFromSteps`, `test_count_missing`) but NOT at Validate.
results.proposal: Close the step-3 residual at Validate. `validateVerifySteps` (skills/src/shared/validate-steps.ts) runs the test command and writes `.datum/last-test-signal.json` with only `{status, exit_code, command, recorded_at}` — verified by reading the file — so an exit-0 run that collected a subset (a stray `-k`/path filter, a partially collected suite) passes the pipeline's final correctness gate on three tests instead of 3731. Add one counting step to that same batch, reusing the lane count gate's counter, and record `test_count` into the signal file from the same shell as `$TEST_EXIT`; then have `datum gate validate` (datum/gate.py:1197) compare it against the count recorded on the epic base. Two named outcomes per principle 3 and the §5 Properties rule: count absent → `validate_count_missing`; count present but below the base → `validate_count_regressed`. Deterministic, no prompt rule, no new agent.
results.where: Validate phase — skills/src/shared/validate-steps.ts (producer) and datum/gate.py `gate_validate` (consumer); test in skills/src/shared/validate-steps.test.ts.
results.rationale: Datum already classifies infra vs code at the moment of failure rather than triaging a mass-red pile afterwards, so six of seven steps are closed defects with named failures; only the exit-0-subset case is genuinely uncovered, and no §5 entry records it, which caps value at 3. Step 6 ("run twice") is deliberately skipped: §6 says `Workflow({resumeFromRunId})` replays every unchanged `agent()`, so a second in-run pass yields no independent sample on resume while doubling the most expensive step, and Validate's independent re-run already supplies the signal.

results.summary: A recon discipline for repos worked on by several machines, sessions or agents at once: fetch and list all refs and open PRs at session start and again immediately before any commit, merge or sequential-identifier claim, so stale snapshots do not cause duplicated work or colliding numbers. It also prescribes one session per working copy, `git -C <path>` with absolute paths and branch checks in subagent prompts, auditing the paths an agent reports, and declaring in-flight branches verbatim when spawning background sessions.
results.origin_incident: PropOS LESSONS_LEARNED: eight incidents of duplicate parallel work and five of edits silently landing in the wrong tree, plus worktree-specific sessions 5, 6 and 44.
results.datum_evidence: Closure "A batch assumed the runner's cwd was the repo root" (4377792d/1a0d0f26): the operator's shell sat in a second worktree of master, every relative path resolved there; closed with setBatchRoot, a guarded cd and `batch_root_missing` — verbatim the skill's wrong-tree class. Plus a8f17108 (writers of a shared file chained in task order, squash order equals write order), principle 6 (scoped commits, lane worktrees strict, `file_ownership_violation`), and the lane-status precondition "worktree is absolute path". Uncovered slice: no recon of the epic tip or remote refs at claim time; main sync happens only at Validate.
results.proposal: Add the "recon immediately before a merge" half only, as a deterministic step, not a prompt rule. The Act boot batch already measures and records `repoRoot` (setBatchRoot); have it also record the epic branch sha, thread it through `phaseArgs` to the act children like `repoRoot`, and add one step to the merge batch in `datum-tdd-act-merge.ts` that re-reads the epic tip before the fold. If the tip moved and not by this run's own landed merges, raise the existing `LaneMergeError` path under a new named failure `epic_tip_moved`, keeping the lanes that landed and writing the reason beside `merge-conflict-<lane>.json`. Do not gate on the mere existence of `<epic>--<task>` refs: a lane branch with no completed marker is the normal re-entry case that lane-level resume consumes (FLOW section 4 and resume mechanism 3), so an existence check would fire on every resume after a failed lane. If a ref scan is wanted instead, scope it to `<epic>--*` refs whose task id is absent from `lane-plan.topological_order`, reusing the "foreign marker" concept from bb673842. The identifier-claim half lands on the already-tracked epic-identity redesign; no separate change.
results.where: Act — `skills/src/shared/boot.ts` (record and thread the epic tip sha alongside repoRoot) and `skills/src/datum-tdd-act-merge.ts` (pre-fold tip re-read plus the `epic_tip_moved` verdict).
results.rationale: Datum already owns the wrong-tree and shared-file-collision halves deterministically (batch_root_missing, chained writers, ownership diffs, per-lane worktrees), so only tip/remote recon at merge time is genuinely missing, and the section 5 defect it maps to is closed rather than open. Datum adds gates from named incidents and no entry records an epic tip moving under a run, so this is worth queuing behind incident-backed work rather than adopting now.

results.summary: Run the actual production build command (not just the test suite) before any commit touching compilation/toolchain, and validate lockfile/toolchain fixes with a clean-room `npm ci` (never `npm install`) since tests can pass under tolerant tooling (ESM under a test runner) while a strict production compile (CommonJS tsc) fails, and node_modules drift hides lockfile staleness until a clean machine hits it.
results.origin_incident: Cited incidents: a Railway/Docker tsc lesson (2026-05-20) and a lessons-learned note (2026-07-19) where tests passed locally but the production build failed under strict compilation, plus lockfile drift only surfacing on a clean install.
results.datum_evidence: FLOW.md §5 Closed, "Lane worktrees had no test environment" (b1634731/97117202/2c39c8c6): lane worktrees get frozen-lockfile installs (`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --prefer-offline`, `uv sync --frozen`) so a lane's environment matches the lockfile, and a missing runner is named `test_env_missing` rather than misread as a red suite. Also §2 Validate: "deterministic re-run of the exact same test command as a batch step" gated on `testExitCode === 0`. But in both places the thing re-run/verified is `config.test_command` — there is no separate production-build command, and no clean-room `npm ci`/frozen-install re-verification step gated specifically on lockfile or build-toolchain changes. Nothing in FLOW.md's Validate contract or Act env-setup distinguishes "tests pass" from "the shipped build compiles," which is exactly the gap this skill targets.
results.proposal: Add a `build_command` field to PipelineConfig (optional; falls back to skipped-and-named when unset) alongside `test_command`. In Validate (docs/FLOW.md §2, the row currently reading "deterministic re-run of the exact same test command as a batch step"), add one more deterministic batch step after the test re-run: if `build_command` is set, run it via the same runBatch path and read its exit code the same way `testExitCode` is read, producing a named `buildExitCode`; a non-zero or null build exit is a new named failure `build_verify_failed` (null distinct from "build is red," same pattern as `validate_run_failed`), and `datum gate validate` requires `buildExitCode === 0` too, not just `testExitCode === 0`. Separately, when the epic diff touches a lockfile path (package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, uv.lock, Pipfile.lock), add a `lockfile-verify` batch step in the same Validate batch that runs the ecosystem's clean-install command (`npm ci`, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `uv sync --frozen`) in a scratch directory checked out from the epic tip, never in the operator's mutated node_modules; a non-zero exit is `lockfile_drift`, read from the step's own exit code exactly like every other batch-derived verdict in Validate.
results.where: Validate phase, docs/FLOW.md §2 "Validate — merged epic → green suite" table (Steps/Gate/Output contract rows) plus the corresponding runtime file (the Validate script under skills/src/, e.g. datum-validate.ts, where the deterministic test re-run batch is built)
results.rationale: The mechanism fits datum's own vocabulary cleanly (a deterministic batch step + named failure feeding `datum gate validate`, never a prompt rule), and datum already has the adjacent pattern (frozen-lockfile installs, exit-code-driven gates) so the addition is cheap. But no FLOW.md §5 closure records an actual incident of "tests green, build red" or "lockfile drift caught only on a clean install" in a datum consumer run, so the value is inferred-applicable rather than evidenced by a recorded defect, keeping it a later-adopt rather than urgent.

results.summary: Mandates that every file:line/commit/date citation in a generated document be mechanically verified by quoting the actual text at that location (via sed/grep/git show/git log --follow) and recorded in a verification table, rather than trusting the model's self-reported "verified" claim; explicit "unverified" declarations are required when a check is skipped.
results.origin_incident: not stated (the skill's own baseline example: 58/62 citations correct on first pass, with confident misattribution of file paths/line numbers/commit dates that self-reported as fully verified)
results.datum_evidence: FLOW.md principle 2/5 and the read_witness closures (K, K2, K3, "witness typo" 65749b10) already implement the identical mechanism — never trust an agent's self-reported claim about file content; verify it against a git blob sha/hash-object — but that verification is applied only to intake reads of the lane-spec file during Act (RED/GREEN/Reflect/Skeptic packets). It is NOT applied to the file:line citations that end up inside human-facing generated artifacts: REVIEW-REPORT.md findings ("dedup by file:line:description", §2 Review — no re-grep of the cited line against the diff), CHANGELOG.md/RETRO.md/CURRENT_STATE.md (Closeout synthesis, §2 Closeout), or FollowUpIssue bodies (validated only against the FollowUpIssue schema shape, per Gap "Single-lens skeptic findings... FollowUpIssue" closure — schema-valid, not content-verified).
results.proposal: Add a deterministic batch step to the Review gate (`datum gate review`, invoked from `skills/src/datum-review.ts` / `shared/gate.ts`) that, for every finding row carrying a `file:line` citation, runs `sed -n '<line>p' <file>` (or an ast-grep/git-show equivalent for commit citations) against the epic diff's worktree and compares it to a short quoted excerpt the finding is required to carry; a citation whose file doesn't exist, whose line is out of range, or whose quoted excerpt doesn't match becomes a named failure `citation_unverified: <lens> <file>:<line>` that the gate reports and blocks on (same shape as `review_severity_unknown`). Extend the same step to Closeout's `closeout-collate`/follow-up filer for any file:line cited in a FollowUpIssue before `datum closeout-file-followups` opens it.
results.where: Review phase gate — skills/src/datum-review.ts and shared/gate.ts (datum gate review); secondarily Closeout — datum/closeout_collate.py / closeout-file-followups path for FollowUpIssue citations
results.rationale: Datum already has the exact enforcing pattern (hash/content-verify an agent's claim rather than trust it — principle 2, the read_witness family of closures) applied to lane-spec reads during Act, but nothing extends that same discipline to file:line citations inside Review findings or Closeout follow-up issues/CHANGELOG, so a fabricated or drifted citation in REVIEW-REPORT.md or a filed GitHub issue would currently pass unchecked. It is a small, well-scoped batch-step addition consistent with FLOW.md's own vocabulary, but no FLOW.md §5 entry records this specific defect occurring yet, so it is a preventive hardening rather than a fix for an observed incident — worth queuing, not urgent.

results.summary: The skill states that every line of code, structural abstraction, and comment must serve a present need — a caller that exists, a reader who learns something the code cannot tell them, or a stated requirement — and gives paired heuristics for structure (avoid speculative abstraction/flexibility) and comments (why-comments only, no narration), while warning against over-correcting into stripped validation or deleted necessary comments.
results.origin_incident: not stated — the skill cites GitClear's 2026 industry data on code duplication/refactoring trends as its empirical motivation, not a specific incident
results.datum_evidence: FLOW.md §2 Review phase already runs four domain lenses (Security, Performance, Architecture, Correctness) whose findings route through the same LLM-proposes/gate-verifies pattern used everywhere else (principle 2), with operator accept/decision persisted and matched by content key (closures fb151ebe, b4276535, ad69a8a6, 3383ff29) rather than a raw self-report. The Architecture lens is the natural home for "unnecessary abstraction/dead code/narrating comments" findings, but the SKILL's specific rule (every line serves a present need; why-comments only) is not named anywhere in FLOW.md's lens descriptions or gap list — it is not a distinct, cited criterion today.
results.proposal: This is a subjective code-quality heuristic, not a computably-verifiable invariant like a test count or exit code — it cannot become a deterministic gate the way principle 2 demands for correctness checks (there's no bash oracle for "does this line serve a present need"). The smallest concrete change is additive to the existing qualitative mechanism, not a new one: add "earn-every-line" as a named criterion string in the Architecture (and/or Correctness) review lens prompt used by datum-review's Act, so findings surface as `(architecture <file>:<line>) unnecessary abstraction/narrating comment`, and let them flow through the review gate's existing content-key accept/decision machinery (same as every other Review finding) — no new batch step, no new gate, no new named failure needed.
results.where: Review phase, the Architecture lens prompt (skills/src/datum-review.ts or wherever the four domain-lens prompts are authored); consumed by the existing `datum gate review` / review-accept flow — no changes to datum/gate.py or lane-steps.ts required.
results.rationale: The skill is a code-quality heuristic for GREEN/REFACTOR-written code, not a pipeline-correctness invariant, and no defect in FLOW.md §5 traces to missing "earn-every-line" enforcement — the closest analogues (#394 dead producers, datum-route dead code) are about datum's own pipeline scripts, not user-code quality, and are already closed by a static consumer test. Because it can't be reduced to a deterministic exit-code gate, the only fit is as one more named criterion inside the Review Architecture lens's existing LLM-proposes/gate-verifies loop — cheap (one prompt line) but low value since nothing forces its use and no recorded incident demanded it.

results.summary: Two-mode skill for removing AI-generation "tells" from code: Build mode pins spec/APIs before generation; Audit mode does (1) execute the code to catch hallucinated API calls, (2) run a mechanical scanner for cosmetic tells (emoji, chat narration, generic names), (3) read the diff for substance issues (tutorial shape, over-engineering, boilerplate, not matching the level surrounding code operates at). It explicitly ranks structural bugs (boilerplate 18.6%, hallucinated APIs 11.2%, over-engineering 7.8%) as far more common than cosmetic tells (emoji 3.9%) and warns against over-correcting toward false "senior" defensiveness.
results.origin_incident: not stated (skill is prescriptive/general, not distilled from a specific datum incident)
results.datum_evidence: Structural "bug" tells the skill names are largely already covered by named datum mechanisms, but nothing addresses cosmetic/over-engineering tells specifically: (1) hallucinated APIs — caught deterministically by Validate's independent test-command re-run and lint step (FLOW.md §2 Validate: 'deterministic re-run of the exact same test command as a batch step... testExitCode(...) === 0'), not by execution-as-audit-step but functionally equivalent; (2) unfinished stubs — the placeholder_assertions gate in RED (FLOW.md §5 closed: 'The placeholder scan read the whole owned file... placeholder_assertions', 440aea1e/7a3c9e44/4d9a182d) matches skeleton-throw shapes, a narrower but analogous mechanical scanner; (3) swallowed exceptions — covered by the general 'No silent fallbacks' principle (FLOW.md principle 3) and its many closures (e.g. 'Closeout swallows tag/archive failures' 2038047/5d2ea00, 'REFACTOR swallowed its reason' a8879a2, the 0ebb74eb silent-fallback sweep). What is NOT covered: a cosmetic-tell scan (emoji, chat artifacts, generic names) and an over-engineering/tutorial-shape/'match surrounding code level' check — no gate, lens, or named failure in FLOW.md addresses these, and Review's four lenses (Security, Performance, Architecture, Correctness) don't include a style/AI-voice/scope-fit lens.
results.proposal: Add a deterministic 'cosmetic-tell scan' batch step (grep/ast-grep over the lane's added-lines diff only, same added-lines-filter technique as the placeholder_assertions fix in 440aea1e to avoid false positives inside strings/fixtures) checking for emoji, common chat-narration phrases ('As an AI', 'Note:', 'I've implemented'), and generic scaffolding names, surfaced as a named non-fatal finding (e.g. cosmetic_tell_found) in the REFACTOR or Review batch — never a hard gate, since these are stylistic. Do not add a deterministic 'over-engineering' or 'matches surrounding code level' check: per FLOW.md principle 2 an LLM may only propose, and over-engineering/tutorial-shape has no mechanical verifier, so at most fold a 'does this match the level of neighboring code, no unrequested defensive layers' instruction into the existing Architecture/Correctness review lens rubric (same treatment as the existing severity rubric in FLOW.md §5's 'Review severity was a hard block' closure) rather than inventing a new gate for something that can't be re-verified deterministically.
results.where: skills/src/datum-tdd-act-lane.ts (post-GREEN/REFACTOR verify batch, alongside strayCleanSteps) for the cosmetic grep scan; skills/src/datum-review.ts lens prompt for the 'match surrounding code level' rubric addition
results.rationale: The skill's own data ranks the parts datum lacks (cosmetics, over-engineering) well below the parts datum already handles (hallucinated APIs via Validate, stubs via placeholder_assertions, swallowed exceptions via principle 3), and FLOW.md §5 records no defect stemming from emoji/chat-artifact/over-engineering leakage, so this isn't preventing a recorded incident — it's a small, cheap, purely additive hygiene check worth queuing but not urgent.

results.summary: Convert every prose invariant ("this is the source of truth", "never auto-populate X", "these must match") into a mechanical, code-level enforcement: byte-identical tests for claimed sources of truth, safety rules encoded as testable functions rather than absence-of-code, drift checks (hashes/CI comparisons) for "must match" guarantees, and verification that a claimed authority actually has importers/consumers. It explicitly does not write the deferred work itself, only turns assertions into verifiable mechanisms.
results.origin_incident: Not stated precisely for datum, but the skill's own cited examples are: a 'source of truth' file with zero importers and stale data, a safety constraint that silently regressed for five weeks, and a design-boundary guarantee with no enforcement mechanism.
results.datum_evidence: The general mechanism is already datum's core design and is enforced far more broadly than the skill proposes: Principle 2 ('An LLM proposes; it never asserts pass/fail... every gate re-runs the check itself as a deterministic datum-cli batch step') is exactly this skill's prescription applied pipeline-wide. Principle 1 ('Every consumer has a producer... a dead field is a bug') covers the skill's 'claimed authority with zero importers' example, closed concretely at FLOW.md line 361 ('datum-route shipped to every consumer with no consumer' -> tests/test_skill_bundles_have_consumers.py now requires every skills/datum-*.js to be dispatched or documented) and line 330 (dead collector producer). Byte-identical/hash drift checks are pervasive: writeFileSteps + git hash-object verification for every LLM-authored artifact (lines 359-369), the read-witness blob-sha verification family (lines 309, 320, 350, 355). Section 5 'Properties' (line 407) literally property-tests the pipeline's own verdict functions so a 'null read as failed' class of bug (the skill's 'safety constraint regressed silently' example) cannot recur. So the general principle is already 'has', not partial. The one real gap: PROPERTIES.md itself (the epic's own SAFETY/INVARIANT/BOUNDARY invariants for the code under construction, phase in FLOW.md section 2 'Properties') is gated only on structural presence -- 'all 11 categories present... and a task traceability table' -- not on whether each claimed invariant is actually backed by a test in the delivered diff. A PROPERTIES.md row can assert a SAFETY invariant that no RED test encodes, and nothing catches that before Validate/Review pass it through as prose.
results.proposal: Add a deterministic check, not a new agent: extend `datum gate properties` (or add a Validate-phase batch step alongside the existing AC-coverage check) that parses PROPERTIES.md's task-traceability table and, for each SAFETY/INVARIANT/BOUNDARY row, requires a cited test file path; a companion batch step in Validate cross-checks that the cited file exists in the epic diff and its test actually ran (present in the same test-command output used for the green-suite gate). A row with no citable test is a named failure (`property_unenforced: <row>`), surfaced the same way `acGaps` is today -- proposal by the Properties-writing agent, verification by the batch, per principle 2.
results.where: Properties phase gate (`datum gate properties`, skills/src/datum-properties.ts) for the citation-presence check; Validate phase (`skills/src/datum-validate.ts`, alongside the existing `acGaps` check) for the test-existence/ran cross-check.
results.rationale: The skill's core mechanism is already the load-bearing idea of datum's whole pipeline (principle 2, the property-tested verdict functions, and the dead-producer/consumer closures at lines 330 and 361), so most of it is already_covered rather than missing. The one uncovered slice -- PROPERTIES.md invariants asserted as prose with no check that a test enforces them -- is not tied to any recorded FLOW.md section-5 defect, so it is a plausible preventive gap worth a small gate addition later, not an urgent one.

results.summary: When plans/commits/discussions defer work ("out of scope," "later," "future work"), place a grep-able code-level anchor (e.g. FORWARD:/TODO: with a decision reference) at the actual file/function/migration where the work will land, plus a decision-log entry — never record the deferral only in a session doc. It only anchors decisions already made to defer; it does not decide whether deferring is appropriate, and .fixme() (not .skip()) keeps expected-breakage tests visible.
results.origin_incident: not stated
results.datum_evidence: datum already has a deterministic deferred-work-tracking mechanism, but it is issue-based, not code-anchor-based: Closeout synthesizes follow-ups "validated against FollowUpIssue before filing" and files them via `datum closeout-file-followups` (§2 Closeout; gap closure "Single-lens skeptic findings were dropped; the follow-up filer had no consumer" — closed in 1052590a/90c8982b/da1be7f0, producing `FollowUpIssue` under `.datum/runs/<run>/follow-ups/<lane>.json`, hash-verified, filed at `--min-severity high`). Review also has an explicit DEFER path: "DEFER lines are accepted by the gate; the carry-forward into the target epic's TICKET is #450" (gap closure 4b6ddf2b/bb5bfaa7).
